items.headline: Rockwood Rocket Tone: 6-Time All-Canadian, and “an Absolute Disaster” as a Sire
items.post_text:
Rockwood Rocket Tone was named All-Canadian six times running. Senior yearling, two-year-old, three-year-old, aged bull. Only two animals in Holstein history ever beat that run.

This was 1949 and the years after, when bull classes still filled the coliseum at the Royal Winter Fair. A champion male could stop traffic on looks alone.

Then his daughters freshened.

E.Y. Morwick, one of the sharpest historians of the breed, needed six words. "A dud, just an absolute disaster." Not as a show bull. As a transmitter.

Andrew Hunt tells the full story in The Bullvine this week, with one number worth keeping. Of the champion bulls of that era, roughly one in six could actually breed.

Those bull classes have since disappeared from the big fairs. The males moved to the sеmen catalogs.

The stage changed. The problem did not. We still weigh what we can see above what we can measure, and the result still lands a season later, on the farm.

When you pick a sire, which of the two is doing more of the work?

#sеmen #cattlebreeding #dairygenetics #holstein

items.headline: Start Where It Hurts: How to Implement Dairy Technology That Scales
items.post_text:
One dairy milked 4,500 cows on two rotary platforms. Its breeding team was ten people per milking.

After installing automated sorting gates, that number dropped to two. Eight people moved to higher-value work. The herd did not shrink. The labor bill did.

Progressive Dairy laid out how this actually happens this week, and the mechanics are worth reading. Sort gates route cows by rule, not by memory. Every cow between 95 and 120 days in milk goes to the hoof trimmer each Wednesday, automatically. Breeding cows and treatment cows separate in a single pass.

The piece makes a quieter point too. The farms that win with technology do not start big. They name their most expensive problem first, missed heats or slow milking or the labor crunch, and solve only that. Then they add one piece at a time, on the same cow IDs.

Most technology is bought before the problem is named. That is the step everyone skips.

What is the one problem you would automate first?

#dairyfarming #precisionlivestock #herdmanagement #agritech
items.summary: The farms that get the most from technology start by naming their most expensive problem – missed heats, slow milking, undetected sick cows or the labor crunch – and solving that first.

items.headline: Many growers still find ‘no meaningful benefit’ from AI use on the farm: survey
items.post_text:
Purdue asked 400 farmers about AI on their operations. More than half, 52%, said the tools provide no meaningful benefit right now.

The detail underneath is sharper than the headline. Agtech usually sells AI as a labor saver. Only 14% of these farmers expected it to cut labor needs or cost. A slightly larger group, 22.8%, thought it would lift production.

Jennifer Marston, writing in AgFunderNews this week, quotes the barometer's lead economist Michael Langemeier. His read is plain. Most respondents simply have not figured out how these tools help their operation yet.

He points to what he calls facts on the ground. A tool can tell you to plant corn on a given day. Weather or a broken machine can make that day impossible.

That last point is the whole story. The barrier is rarely belief in the technology. It is whether the technology survives the conditions of a real working day.

What would it take for a tool to earn a permanent place on your operation?

#agritech #livestock #precisionag #farmtech

items.headline: Holstein’s 60-Inch Rule: Why Breeders Are Backing It With 53%-vs-21% Math
items.summary: Two weeks after the May 2026 stature penalty, breeders answered back with heritability math: 53% vs 21%.
items.post_text:
Two weeks after Holstein USA's new stature penalty landed, docking cows over 60 inches, the sharpest response wasn't outrage. It was a heritability lesson. Andrew Hunt, writing in The Bullvine this week, traces how one comment reframed the debate.

Quebec breeder Emeric Lebacle made the point almost in passing: stature runs about 53% heritable by Lactanet's numbers, while feet and legs sit around 21% for the major score. Push hard on a low-heritability trait and progress crawls. Stature responds roughly 2.5 times more reliably to selection.

The penalty bites gradually: no deduction at 60 inches, minus 0.15 at 61, climbing to minus 3.45 at 70. Taller cows tend to exit the herd earlier, and an early cull costs roughly $2,000 per replacement heifer.

Feet and legs stay weak even in today's top GTPI bulls, and the penalty doesn't fix that directly. A short cow once denied an "Excellent" score became one of Wisconsin's highest lifetime milk producers.

Where would you draw the line between structural durability and chasing a number on paper?

#genetics #Holstein #dairybreeding #heritability #cattlegenetics

items.headline: Increase breeding results with synch protocols and estrus detection aids
items.summary: Latest synchronization protocols and estrus detection aids for greater reproductive success.
items.post_text:
Half or more of your cows can be noncycling when a synch protocol starts.

That number comes from Jordan Thomas, writing in Progressive Cattle this week, and it gets worse after a long calving season. A synchronized cow that never shows heat is a wasted shot.

The Beef Reproduction Task Force publishes validated protocol sheets every year. For heifers not yet cycling, longer progestin protocols like the 14-day CIDR-prostaglandin give more time to reach puberty. For cows, the classic is 7-day Cosynch plus CIDR, with a newer 7 & 7 Synch variant adding an extra prostaglandin dose.

Breeding indicator patches add a decision layer on top. If 50% or more of the patch ink rubs off, that female is a strong candidate for sexed sеmen. Less than half, and conventional sеmen may be safer.

So much of this rides on what happens before insemination. Detection is what tells you whether the protocol worked at all.

Are estrus detection aids underused on your operation, or already standard?

#reproduction #cattlebreeding #ArtificialInsemination #sеmen #dairygenetics

items.headline: Your Oldest Cow Isn't a Cull — She's a $3,000 Heifer You Don't Have to Buy
items.summary: Replacement heifer costs hit $3,010/head, up 164% since 2019, making cow longevity an economic strategy; reproductive health (clearing uterine infections) is one of four pillars keeping cows productive longer.
items.post_text:
Keeping cows one extra lactation saves a 200-cow dairy about $60,000 a year.

That is the math Andrew Hunt lays out in The Bullvine this week, and it starts with what a replacement costs. A dairy heifer now runs $3,010, up from $1,140 in April 2019. Top auction prices in California and Minnesota have crossed $4,000.

The national average is 2.7 lactations. Move it to 3.7 and that herd raises roughly 20 fewer heifers a year. Buying your way out is getting harder. USDA counted 3.914 million replacement heifers this January, the lowest since 1978.

Hunt names four pillars behind the extra lactation: transition nutrition, udder health, foot care, and reproductive health, specifically clearing uterine infections across consecutive cycles.

The ceiling is higher than most herds imagine. Gillette Emperor Smurf EX-91, a Holstein in her 18th lactation, has produced 478,163 pounds of milk, a Guinness World Record.

The fourth pillar is where fertility work quietly pays for itself.

What's the oldest cow still earning her keep in your herd, and what's actually keeping her there?

#reproduction #dairyfarming #cattlebreeding #cowlongevity #dairyeconomics

items.headline: Does delaying conception improve profitability?
items.summary: Study on dry period length and days open: intermediate-length dry periods gave higher milk production and better fertility; questions whether delaying conception in high-producing modern Holsteins improves profitability.
items.post_text:
Delaying conception does not pay off, not even in the highest-producing herds.

That is the finding from a retrospective study by Overton and Eicker covering more than 109,000 Holstein cows across 60 US dairy herds, reported this week by Alvaro Garcia in Progressive Dairy.

The question was reasonable. Modern Holsteins hold their lactation curve longer than cows a generation ago, so some producers wondered whether longer days open would mean more milk before pregnancy took its toll.

The data said otherwise. Longer days open in one lactation raised replacement risk in the next. Dry period length followed a curve, not a line: both too short and too long raised early-removal risk, with roughly 60 days best. Cows that conceived earlier and kept a traditional dry period made more milk through 90 days and got pregnant sooner next lactation.

Garcia's conclusion is that reproductive efficiency is not a pregnancy checkbox. It is a long-term driver of survivability and profit.

Where is your herd's dry period landing, and does it match what the cow's transition needs?

#dairy #reproduction #cattle #fertility #herdhealth

items.headline: New technology, new possibilities: How to introduce artificial intelligence into your dairy
items.summary: CATTLEytics founder Shari van de Pol explains how AI helps producers with data analytics, breeding schedules, nutrition, disease diagnosis and employee management on dairies of any size.
items.post_text:
The dairy AI problem is not collecting data but acting on it, and the fix starts with one question, not the whole farm.

That is Shari van de Pol, a computer engineer turned large-animal vet, on the Progressive Dairy Podcast in a piece by Patryce Eldredge LeFevre this week. "You can have all the information in the world, but if you're not actually making any changes, what's the point?"

Van de Pol founded CATTLEytics around exactly that gap. Her method is unglamorous. Open ChatGPT, Copilot or Perplexity. Ask a real question about your operation. If the answer feels off, push back and ask it to refine.

She is clear about the limits. AI does not replace the nutritionist or the vet. It fills gaps and spots patterns across feed, breeding and health records. She also sees it as a leveler, giving smaller operations analysis only large dairies could afford.

The tool is only as useful as the question you bring it.

What is the one recurring decision you would hand to AI first?

#dairy #AI #agtech #dataanalytics #cattle

items.headline: Orbem begins US rollout of MRI-based in-ovo sexing tech
items.summary: German startup Orbem, backed by 55.5M euro Series B, deploys MRI+AI system determining chick sex in-ovo with 99.5% accuracy in under a second; first US hatchery system live, second in mid-August; in-ovo sexing already covers 40% of EU commercial layer flock.
items.post_text:
An MRI scanner can now sex a chick inside the egg with 99.5% accuracy, in under a second.

Orbem's system is running at its first US hatchery, according to AgFunderNews this week. The Munich-founded startup, with a Texas office since 2025, calls it "Genus Focus": an MRI scanner paired with AI that identifies a chick's developing reproductive organs around day 11 to 12 of incubation.

A second US installation is scheduled for mid-August, a third for 2027. Jennifer Volz, the company's head of global business development, says a major US retailer will announce its own rollout soon.

Europe got there first. In-ovo sexing already covers 40% of the EU's commercial layer flock, and more than 281 million female chicks have been selected this way since 2021. Orbem runs the system as pay-per-use rather than selling hardware, and reports being profitable after a 55.5 million euro Series B in January.

Sex determination before birth, at near-perfect accuracy, keeps showing up as the economics driver across species. Where else in animal agriculture is this precision still missing?

#agritech #genetics #AI #innovation #poultry

items.headline: Creating pregnancies in the heat with Ben Dickman
items.summary: Podcast transcript: Arizona dairy Dickman and Sons raised its summer 21-day pregnancy rate from the low teens to about 20% after a four-year cooling system investment, using CowManager activity monitoring, an 80-day voluntary waiting period, sexed and beef semen, and genomic culling.
items.post_text:
An Arizona dairy pushed its summer pregnancy rate from the low teens to roughly 20%, and the cooling starts in March.

Ben Dickman, third-generation owner of Dickman and Sons Dairy in Coolidge, told Progressive Dairy editor Matti McBride the farm hit 105°F that early this year. Nights still run from the high 90s into triple digits.

The 3,600-cow dairy uses exit lane drenches, flip fans and manger drenchers tied to humidity, dew point and wind. Four years in, it paid for itself in a year and a half, not the projected three.

Reproduction runs on an 80-day voluntary waiting period and CowManager monitoring, aiming to get sеmen into every cow by 99 days in milk. Genomics decide who stays: low scorers get culled, sexed sеmen goes to heifers, beef sеmen to second-lactation-plus cows, and the bottom 20% is sold twice a year.

Most heat-stress conversations focus on the animal in the moment. Dickman's numbers point to an infrastructure bet made years before the heat arrived.

What payback horizon does your dairy budget for cooling investments?

#dairyreproduction #hеatstress #cattlebreeding #genomics #dairyfarming

items.headline: Exclusive: Calysta hires new CEO, seeks new capital as JV partner ends financial support
items.summary: Gas fermentation firm Calysta brought in new CEO Berend Jan Kingma after its China JV partner Adisseo ended financial support and halted production at the Chongqing single-cell protein plant; Calysseo 2025 unaudited results show $78.7M assets, $63.9M liabilities, $710k revenue and a $15.5M net loss.
items.post_text:
A single-cell protein plant that booked $710,000 in revenue and a $15.5 million loss has stopped production.

It belongs to Calysseo, the joint venture between gas-fermentation company Calysta and animal nutrition group Adisseo, in Chongqing, China. Elaine Watson, writing in AgFunderNews, reported that Adisseo told the Shanghai Stock Exchange on June 18 it would not renew a loan to the venture after a failed bid for outside financing, citing a "severe shortage of working capital."

Adisseo warned the plant needed "substantial and sustainable financial support" to resume upgrades. Calysseo's unaudited 2025 numbers: $78.7 million in assets, $63.9 million in liabilities.

Calysta has a new CEO, Berend Jan Kingma, formerly of InspiraFarms, FirstWave Group and Miro Forestry. Cofounder Alan Shaw, now non-executive chair, told AgFunderNews the focus is "debottlenecking downstream processing" to raise the capital the plant needs.

Turning methane into feed protein for aquaculture and petfood was a capital-intensive bet. This is what it costs to learn whether the science scales before the money runs out.

Does the science need more time, or more money?

#agritechdeals #alternativeprotein #feedtech #agtechfunding #startups

items.headline: Key performance areas to focus on with automated milking systems
items.post_text:
A robotic milking herd's ideal average is 145 to 160 days in milk, and only strong breeding keeps it there.

Jason French, Commercial Portfolio Manager at DeLaval North America, laid out the math in Progressive Dairy this week.

Automated milking performance splits into two sides. On the cow side, producers set traffic rules: cows in their first 100 days of lactation get more robot visits, cows nearing dry-off get fewer. Hitting that 145 to 160 day window needs strong reproductive performance behind it.

Activity monitors and progesterone testing feed that side, sharpening heat detection and breeding accuracy so fresh cows keep entering the herd on schedule.

On the robot side, French sets his own bar: incomplete milkings should stay in the low single digits, and higher peak milk flow should keep box time short, since box time caps how many cows a robot handles daily.

The two dashboards rarely get read together, though they track the same herd.

Which one gets checked more often on your farm, the cow numbers or the robot numbers?

#dairyfarming #automatedmilking #reproduction #precisionlivestock #dairytech

items.headline: New genetic tools could match bulls to your farm's environment
items.summary: University of Tennessee beef specialist Troy Rowan and land-grant researchers, with the American Angus Association, are developing genetic-by-environment (GxE) tools and adaptive indicator traits like hair shedding scores, aiming to rebuild EPDs with satellite climate data so bull genetics match local heat and forage conditions instead of an assumed average.
items.post_text:
A top bull's genetics do not perform the same in Florida and in Montana, and most breeding tools still assume they do.

Raney Rapp writes about this in Farm Progress this week. Researchers are studying genetic by environment interaction, or GxE: the idea that a sire's genetic value shifts with climate and management.

University of Tennessee beef specialist Troy Rowan put it plainly. Average environments don't exist and average management doesn't exist.

Artificial insemination made elite genetics available everywhere. It also erased traits that helped cattle handle heat or poor forage at home. One early fix already works: hair shedding scores that gauge heat and fescue tolerance.

Land grant universities and the American Angus Association are going further. They are rebuilding expected progeny differences, the scorecards breeders use to pick sires. The new versions will add satellite climate data and real farm records.

Selection tools are moving past breed and carcass numbers, toward genetics matched to the farm they will actually work on.

Would knowing your bull's GxE profile change which sire you buy next?

#cattlegenetics #beefcattle #EPD #genomics #cattlebreeding
items.author: Raney Rapp

items.headline: The $1,300 Gap Between the Bull You Want and the Bull You Should Buy
items.summary: Bullvine analysis of Canada's 20 most-used Holstein sires found some rank 96th percentile for overall LPI but only 31st for Health & Welfare, which is just 8% of the index; Lactanet Pro$ data and a US DWP$ validation put the gap at roughly $1,300 in lifetime profit per daughter, driven by differences in lameness and mastitis rates.
items.post_text:
A 96th-percentile LPI bull can rank 31st for health, a $1,300 gap per daughter.

Murray Hunt writes about it in The Bullvine this week. LPI is Lactanet's genetic merit index for Holstein sires in Canada. Hunt checked the country's 20 most-used sires against its six new subindexes. Some bulls sat at the 96th percentile overall but ranked only 31st for Health and Welfare.

Health and Welfare carries 8% of the total score, next to Production at 40% and Longevity and Type at 32%. Top-quartile sires for health keep 7.4% more daughters at six years, worth $1,300 more per daughter. Their daughters show 15.9 points less lameness and 14.9 points less mastitis.

Hunt calls the composite score a flattering headshot: one number, easy to post and sell. He says the subindexes are the scan that shows where the joint is failing.

A composite score is built to average. Averaging is what hides the one weak trait that costs the most later.

How many of your last sire purchases would survive a look at their subindexes alone?

#Holstein #dairygenetics #cattlebreeding #geneticselection #Lactanet
